title: The Greatest: How a Kid from Louisville Shook Up the World
shortDescription: Born Cassius Marcellus Clay Jr in Louisville, Kentucky on 17 January 1942, a talkative twelve-year-old who lost nothing but a stolen bicycle and found the sport that would remake his life, he flew to the 1960 Rome Olympics at eighteen and came home a gold medallist — then 'shook up the world' by beating the fearsome Sonny Liston in 1964, changed his name and his religion the moment it mattered most, and gave up the heavyweight crown at the height of his fame rather than fight in a war he believed was wrong. He fought his way back to become a three-time world heavyweight champion, lit the Olympic flame in Atlanta in 1996, and lived long enough to be called, almost without anyone disputing it, the most famous person who ever lived.
introduction: Cassius Marcellus Clay Jr was born in Louisville, Kentucky, on 17 January 1942, the son of a sign painter and a housekeeper in a city where the colour line still ran through everything — he would grow up to say that he and his brother were taught by their mother to love people, no matter their colour, and by their father the hard truth of what the world would do to them because of theirs. He was a boy who loved to talk. He ran through the streets of Louisville West End at night with his father waiting up for him, and he walked to school past the segregated drinking fountains. When he was twelve, someone stole his brand-new bicycle — a red-and-white Schwinn his father had bought him for a down payment on a church lot — and a furious little boy went looking for the thief, determined to give him a whipping. A police officer and boxing trainer named Joe Martin heard the twelve-year-old threaten to whoop whoever had taken his bike intelligence. 'Well,' Martin said, 'you better learn how to fight first.' The boy was in the gym before the week was out. His mouth guaranteed it, his legs would decide it, and his hands would settle the argument — and the argument would turn out to be with the whole century.

chapters.heading: A tiresome kid who never shut up — and the gold medal in Rome
paragraphs: Cassius Clay discovered that he had a talent no one expected. He was quick, impossibly quick — he was given the nickname 'the Louisville Lip' in the amateur ranks, not just because he talked so much, but because he seemed to be mobile on top of a torrent of words. Trainers said that he was very fast with his hands even as a kid; he had a lightning-fast jab that was truly jolting to the pro body. He trained by running to school, running home, and running (not driving) past the bus stop; his roadwork became the thing that separated him from every other heavyweight. He fought at light-heavyweight in the 1960 Rome Olympics and won the gold medal, beating Zbigniew Pietrzykowski of Poland in the final by decision, and the world's press noticed a nineteen-year-old who could not stop talking about himself. He looked at the sky and told reporters he was the greatest, and every one of them laughed at him. He meant it, every word.

He turned professional in 1960 on the advice of his Louisville friends, a group of wealthy white businessmen who were impressed by how much attention he had drawn in Romepisodes The Louisville Sponsoring Group paid him a salary and gave him a road to the title. His style was entirely wrong for a heavyweight — he was tall and skinny, he moved on the balls of his feet like a dancer, he carried his hands far too low, and he talked so much during the fight that referees occasionally asked him to stop. But the box he had invented for himself, a dancing jab-and-run style with a snapping left, was built to exploit exactly what heavyweight history thought was impossible: that a big man could box like a featherweight and still hit like a truck. Between Rome and the title he ran through a string of opponents — turning on professional records, selling out arenas, and talking so much that sports writers who hated him (and there were many) had to admit that whatever else he was, he was never boring. He even predicted the round in which he would knock his opponents out, and to the delight of the crowd and the fury of the press, he was usually right.

By early 1964 the talk had become impossible to ignore. The world's heavyweight champion was a 240-pound former convict named Sonny Liston, a hulking, intimidating man with fists the size of dinner plates, a fearsome right hand, and a reputation so terrifying that most of the sport's best contenders had literally chosen to leave the ring rather than face him. Clay was the one challenger who was not afraid. On 25 February 1964, at the Convention Hall in Miami Beach, the twenty-two-year-old put eleven words on the record that would change his life: 'I am the best. I shook up the world.'

The boxing establishment had predicted disaster. Liston was a 7-to-1 favourite; everyone assumed the talkative kid's legs would give out, or that his jaw could not hold the punch of a monster. Instead, at 11:41 p.m. on 25 February 1964, in a fight that lasted only a few rounds — with the world listening on radio because the championship had not been put on live television — Clay broke Liston down with his impossible legs and a jab so snapping that Liston, bleeding and allergic to the stinging blows, refused to come out for round seven, saying his shoulder had been injured. Cassius Clay had done it. At eight o'clock the next morning he announced that his name was now Muhammad Ali, that he had found his religion, and that he was the king of the world. He had, in a single night, shaken every assumption about what a heavyweight — and what an American — was allowed to be.

media.alt: Cassius Clay (light-heavyweight) at the 1960 Rome Olympics
media.caption: Eighteen-year-old Cassius Clay at the Rome Olympics, weeks before he came home with the light-heavyweight gold.

chapters.heading: 'I shook up the world' — the night he became the champion
paragraphs: If the sport had expected Liston to crush the young pretender, the first round refuted them all. For the entire fight Clay displayed a kind of movement heavyweight fans had never witnessed. He stayed on his toes for the full distance, snapped jabs that Liston never fully solved, and — most infamously — kept shouting insults from inside the ring: 'You're too ugly, big bear! Get up and fight, you big ugly bear!' Liston, a man who had built a career on terrifying his opponents, was reduced to swinging wild, powerful, unanswerable punches that kept catching air. In the third round something strange happened: Liston's eye began to swell and burn, reportedly because the ointment from Clay's corner had worked its way into the champion's eyes. For a few rounds the monster looked merely human. By the sixth, Liston was exhausted, halfway to beaten; he sat on his stool at the end of the sixth round, told his cornermen his shoulder had gone, and never got up for the seventh. The fight was over. Cassius Clay, twenty-two years old, had 'shook up the world,' and he screamed it into the microphone so that the whole planet heard: 'I shook up the world! I shook up the world!'

The rematch was one of the strangest spectacles in boxing history, and it produced a single photograph that would outlast every other image of him. On 25 May 1965, in the tiny town hall auditorium of Lewiston, Maine — a venue so small that reporters outnumbered the crowd — Ali and Liston squared off again. In the very first round, Ali threw a short, seemingly gentle right hand that has gone down in legend as the 'phantom punch' because so few people actually saw it land. Liston went down hard onto his back and lay there, and Ali stood over the fallen giant shouting 'Get up and fight, you big ugly bear!' The photograph of Ali standing imperiously over the sprawled Liston, arms raised, is one of the most reproduced sports pictures ever taken, and it froze forever the exact instant the old era ended and the Ali era began. He had beaten the impossible man twice. There was no argument left: this was his era now.

media.alt: Muhammad Ali and Sonny Liston during their first fight in Miami Beach, 1964
media.caption: February 1964, Miami Beach: the young challenger snapping his jab past the fearsome champion.

chapters.heading: The name, the religion, and the crown he would not give to a war
paragraphs: Almost nobody in America knew what to make of the new champion. He was a Muslim — a Black Muslim, in the language of the day — and he had changed his name from 'Cassius Clay,' which he called his 'slave name,' to Muhammad Ali, which he said meant 'Beloved of God.' The sports establishment fumed. White America, which had loved the safe, smiling, patriotic Cassius Clay, was bewildered by the new champion who refused to be the polite negro and who said, over and over, 'I don't have to be what you want me to be.' He proved himself the most extraordinary talker in the history of the ring — 'Float like a butterfly, sting like a bee, his hands can't hit what his eyes can't see' — and then he won, and kept winning. He defended his title against former champion Floyd Patterson, against George Chuvalo, Henry Cooper, and Brian London, and against almost every contender the sport could send at him. He beat them all, and made it look easy.

But the era was closing in on him. The United States had been drafting young men to fight in Vietnam since the mid-1960s, and the war was growing more unpopular with every passing month. When Ali's name was called, in the spring of 1967, he was given a chance to do what most celebrities did — to accept a cushy assignment, to go to Vietnam as a sports ambassador, to appear in patriotic newsreels. He refused. On 28 April 1967, in Houston, Texas, he stood before the board and answered 'I will not go ten thousand miles from home to help murder and burn another poor nation simply to continue the domination of white slave masters of the darker people of the earth.' For that refusal he was stripped of his title, his boxing licence, and his passport, and indicted for draft evasion — a crime carrying five years in prison and a $10,000 fine. The heavyweight champion of the world, at twenty-five, at the absolute peak of his powers, was reduced to giving speeches on college campuses, some of which were heckled by protesters of the war he was opposing. He lost three of the best years of his career. He never once said he regretted it.

The decision cost him almost everything, and it defined him forever. While he was out of the ring, the civil rights movement and the anti-war movement made common cause in a way no one had predicted, and Ali became one of the great faces of both. White America's anger at him — the newspaper columnists who called him a traitor, the boxing commissions that banned him in every state, the government that took his livelihood — slowly curdled into something else: respect, and then awe, at a man so principled he would give up a fortune rather than be ordered around his conscience. He would later say, 'I never thought of losing, but now that it's real I realize that it's worth fighting for, even at the cost of everything I have.' He meant every word.

In June 1971, the Supreme Court of the United States ruled unanimously in Clay v. United States that Ali's conviction for refusing the draft was unlawful — the Court found the government had improperly instructed the jury that his beliefs were not sincerely held because he had said his reasons were 'religious' when he had originally stated them as both religious and political. By then the war was bleeding to a close, the country had turned against it, and Ali, at last, was free to fight again. He was no longer young. The years of exile had taken his prime, and the monster who had beaten everyone while Ali was away — a relentless slugger named Joe Frazier — stood in his way.

media.alt: Muhammad Ali in 1967, the year he refused the draft
media.caption: 1967: the champion stripped of his title, his licence and his passport for refusing to fight in Vietnam.

chapters.heading: The Rumble in the Jungle — the comeback of the century
paragraphs: By 1971, Ali was back in the ringcolon But the man who returned was no longer invincible. Joe Frazier, the undefeated champion who had won the title while Ali was in exile, met him at Madison Square Garden on 8 March 1971 in 'the Fight of the Century,' and in a brutal fifteen-round war Frazier knocked Ali down and beat him on points. Ali's jaw was broken by Frazier's huge left hook; the world watched the unbeaten legend finally lose, and for a moment it looked like the exile had cost him his myth. Everyone told him to retire. He refused. He fought Frazier again in 1974 and won a rematch by decision, and then he set his eyes on the biggest prize of all.

In October 1974 he went to Zaire, in central Africa, to fight George Foreman — the terrifying young champion who had knocked out Joe Frazier in two rounds and Ken Norton in the first, a man considered virtually unbeatableiak. Foreman was seven years younger, forty pounds heavier, and a 2-to-1 favourite; most observers thought Ali would be destroyed. In the city of Kinshasa, in a stadium built for the occasion, Ali did something no one had ever seen a heavyweight do. He leaned back on the ropes and let Foreman punch himself out. For round after round he absorbed Foreman's heaviest shots, taunting the exhausted giant with 'You better move, you big ugly bear!' The tactic — later called the 'rope-a-dope' — was a calculated gamble: all of Ali's genius wrapped in a disguise of weakness. In the eighth round, with Foreman spentaaa one of the heaviest hitters in history mustered the only thing he had left — one great right hand — and Ali, perfectly calm, put him down and out. 'Ali, boma ye! Ali, bomaye!' — 'Ali, kill him!' — the crowd screamed all night, and on 30 October 1974 Muhammad Ali knocked out George Foreman in the eighth round in what is still called the most famous boxing match of the twentieth century: the Rumble in the Jungle. He had lost everything, gone away for three years, come back and been beaten, and then, against the youngest, strongest, most dangerous heavyweight alive, he had taken his championship back at the age of thirty-two. The whole world was roaring.

He would do it once more. After losing his title to Leon Spinks in 1978, he regained it in a rematch the same year, becoming the first man in history to win the heavyweight championship three times — and earning, in the words of the sportswriters who had once hated him, a place not just in boxing but in the imagination of the world. He retired in 1979, came back for two final, sad, slow fights, and in 1981 finally hung up his gloves for good.

media.alt: Muhammad Ali at the Rumble in the Jungle, Zaire, 1974
media.caption: October 1974, Kinshasa, Zaire: Ali, on the ropes and taunting, beats the unbeatable George Foreman in eight rounds.

chapters.heading: The shaking hands that lit the flame — legacy of a legend
paragraphs: Muhammad Ali's last great public moment came on the evening of 19 July 1996, in Atlanta, Georgia, at the opening ceremony of the Centennial Olympic Games. Parkinson's disease — the same cruel neurological illness that had taken his speech and his steadiness in the years after his retirement — had been quietly stealing parts of him since the early 1980s, and it was no secret that the man who had once been the fastest and most graceful heavyweight in history now moved slowly, his hands trembling, his face set in the fixed expression the disease gives so many of its victims. The world had watched him decline for a decade and a half, and it ached for him. Then America, and the whole planet, watched him do the one thing no one could have scripted: the trembling, visibly shaking hands of the old champion reached up, took the sacred Olympic torch from the runner, and lit the flame that opened the 1996 Atlanta Games while a billion people held their breath and wept exactly as he had made half the world weep in the ring — but this time, alone and without gloves, standing perfectly still in the light of the whole world's respect. It may be the single most famous gesture of gratitude in modern Olympic history: the torch that Muhammad Ali's pale, shaking hand lit not for the glory of winning but as a declaration that Parkinson's had not beaten him any more than Liston, or the draft board, or George Foreman ever had.

He used the years that followed to do the work of the last legend: the Muhammad Ali Center opened in Louisville in 2005 to teach the world his values — respect, confidence, conviction, dedication, giving, spirituality — and to inspire the young, and to prove to every child who felt powerless that the power to change the world starts exactly where Ali started, with one small hand raised over a stolen bicycle insisting, 'I am the greatest.' He died on 3 June 2016, at the age of seventy-four, in Scottsdale, Arizona, of complications of his Parkinson's disease. The funeral in Louisville — his chosen home — followed a route through the streets of his childhood, past the places where a talkative boy had once learned to fight; and it was watched by hundreds of millions of people around the world, who lined the streets of his city and called out the old words: 'Ali, bomaye!' Ali has been dead since 2016, but he has not been forgotten: he remains, by any measure, the most famous person of the twentieth century — the man who shook up the world.
